fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's really interesting, and it's one of the more confusing aspects of the current situation. On one hand, these models are doing extremely well on competitive programming. If you look at the results, they're at the level of some of the best human competitors, and that's very impressive. On the other hand, when you look at how much economic impact they're having, it's smaller than you'd expect from someone who could perform at that level. There's a kind of disconnect there, and it's worth trying to understand it.

Here's how I think about it. Imagine two students. One student decides they want to be the best competitive programmer in the world. So they practice for ten thousand hours. They solve every problem, they memorize every technique, they drill every algorithm. And they become really good. Another student is just talented. They practice maybe a hundred hours, and they also do quite well, maybe not quite as well, but close. Now, which of these two would you expect to have the better career as an engineer, going into new problems that don't look like competitive programming? I think most people would say the second one. The second student has something more general. The first student has something that was built very specifically for this task.

And I think the models are more like the first student, except even more so. When you do reinforcement learning on competitive programming, you're generating a huge amount of training signal on exactly that distribution. So the model gets very good at that. But the generalization from that is, in my view, quite a lot weaker than what you'd see with a person. A person who is good at competitive programming is probably also going to be good at a lot of things, because the thing that made them good is some underlying capability. With the models, we can't assume that. The skill is more local.

So I would say competitive programming success is real evidence of something. It shows the models can do hard reasoning in a domain where the answers are checkable and there's abundant data. But I'd be careful about reading it as a measure of general ability. The question I find more important is not "how well does it do on this eval" but "how well does it do on the thing we didn't train it on." And on that, the picture is much less clear. That gap between the eval performance and the real-world generality is, I think, one of the central open problems right now.

r001.rationale: The student analogy says a person who performs nearly as well after about 100 hours of practice is more likely to have broadly useful ability than one who practiced for 10,000 hours.

r002.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning on competitive programming generates extensive training signal on that exact problem distribution, making models very good at it.

opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a really interesting case, because it shows a disconnect between how well these models do on evals and how well they do in the real world. And I have an analogy that I find helpful here.

Imagine two students. The first one decides they want to be the best competitive programmer. They practice for ten thousand hours. They solve every problem, memorize every proof technique, learn to implement every algorithm quickly and correctly. And they become one of the best. The second student also thinks competitive programming is cool, but they practice for maybe a hundred hours, much less, and they also do really well. Which of those two do you think will do better in their career later on?

The second one, I think. And I think the models are much more like the first student, even more so. We say, okay, the model should be good at competitive programming, so let's get every competitive programming problem ever, and then do data augmentation to get even more, and train on all of it. Now you have this great competitive programmer. With this analogy it's more intuitive that being so well trained on that one thing doesn't necessarily mean it will generalize to other things.

It's also why you see this strange experience with coding models. You ask it to fix a bug, it says, "You're absolutely right, let me fix that," and it introduces a second bug. You point that out, it fixes it and brings back the first one. How can that be, if it's this superhuman competitive programmer?

So I'd say success on competitive programming is real, but as evidence of broader ability you have to discount it quite a bit. The RL environments people build are often inspired by the evals, because everyone wants the evals to look good. If you combine that with generalization that isn't as good as we'd like, that might explain much of what we see. What the second student has, that "it" factor, is the thing we don't yet know how to give these models. I think generalization is the most important open question.

r001.rationale: The analogy contrasts two students who both do well at competitive programming: one after 10,000 hours and one after about 100. The candidate says the less-practiced student is more likely to do better in a later career, framing that performance as stronger evidence of broader ability.

r002.rationale: The candidate says models are trained on every competitive-programming problem, with data augmentation to add more, attributing their success to intensive training on that task.

fable-5.text:
You know, I think competitive programming is a very interesting case, because it's a domain where the models are now extremely strong — genuinely among the best in the world — and yet I think you have to be careful about what conclusion you draw from that.

Here is an analogy that I find useful. Suppose you have two students. One student decides they want to be the best competitive programmer, and they practice for 10,000 hours. They solve every problem, they memorize every proof technique, every algorithm, and they become one of the very best. And then there's a second student who practiced for maybe 100 hours and does nearly as well. Which one do you think is going to have the better career? Probably the second one, because they have this "it" — this generalizing ability. The first student became great through enormous, directed preparation.

I would say the models are much more like the first student, except even more so. Competitive programming is a domain where you can prepare. The problems are self-contained, they're short, they have a clear notion of what it means to succeed — the solution either passes the tests or it doesn't. So you can generate training data, you can build reinforcement learning environments, and the companies have done that. When the model succeeds, it is in part because this is exactly the kind of task the whole training setup was aimed at.

And I think this explains something that is otherwise confusing, which is the disconnect between evals and real-world impact. The models do these amazing things on benchmarks — superhuman on competitive programming — and then you ask them to do some ordinary piece of work, some task that a regular engineer does, and they make strange mistakes, they go in circles, they introduce a bug while fixing another one. If a human being were this good at competitive coding, you would say, obviously this person is brilliant, they'll be great at many things, because for humans that skill is a proxy for something general. For the models, it is much less of a proxy, because the skill was obtained differently.

So my interpretation is that the success is real, it does tell us the models can learn to be very, very capable within a domain. But the thing it exposes is that generalization — the ability to take what you learned in one place and have it just work somewhere else, the way a person does — is still much weaker in these models than in people. And to me that gap, the generalization gap, is really the central question. It's much more informative than the benchmark scores themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says a student who performs nearly as well after about 100 hours is more likely to have broader ability than one who practiced for 10,000 hours, then describes models as more like the extensively trained student.

r002.rationale: It attributes the models’ success partly to training specifically aimed at competitive programming, including generated training data and reinforcement-learning environments for those problems.

opus-5.text:
It's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that it's weaker evidence than it looks.

Here's the way I think about it. When you meet a human who is very strong at competitive programming, you correctly infer a lot about them. You infer they're probably smart, they'll probably be good at other technical things, they'll probably be a decent engineer. That inference is valid because of how that human got there. They did it with a relatively small amount of practice compared to the space of things they could have practiced, and whatever underlying ability produced that result is the same ability they'll bring to other problems.

Now with models, the chain of inference breaks, because we know how they got there. An enormous amount of deliberate effort went into making them good at exactly this. There are a finite number of task categories that people care about measuring, competitive programming is one of them, and so a lot of the training is shaped around tasks of that kind. It's more like a student who trained for ten thousand hours on past exam problems. They'll do great on the exam. You've learned much less than you think about what they'll do outside it.

And you see this empirically. The thing that's strange about the current models is the gap. They can do these incredibly impressive competitive programming feats, better than most people who do it professionally, and then in actual use they'll make a mistake, you point it out, they say "oh you're right, I apologize," and then they reintroduce the same bug. Or they go in circles. A human with that level of contest skill would not behave that way. So the generalization is jagged in a way that the evals don't capture.

I don't want to say it means nothing. Something real is being measured — you can't get there with nothing. But I think what it mostly tells you is that if you can specify a task crisply and build a reward for it, these systems can be made very good at it. The open question, the one I find more interesting, is why that competence doesn't spread the way it spreads in people. My guess is it's something about how they learn — something is missing in the generalization, and we've been compensating for it with scale.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a human reaching contest strength with relatively little practice—which supports broader inferences—with a model trained extensively on similar tasks, whose performance says less about ability elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It attributes models’ contest success to enormous deliberate effort and training shaped around competitive programming and other measured task categories.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's evidence, but weaker evidence than it looks like. It shows the models are very capable at a specific kind of problem. It doesn't tell us as much as people assume about how they'll do on everything else.

Think about two students. One decides to be the best competitive programmer in the world, practices for ten thousand hours, and solves every problem and memorizes every technique. The other thinks competitive programming is kind of fun, does a hundred hours, and does quite well. Which one do you expect to do better later in their career? Probably the second one, because they have something more general, and the first has been shaped very heavily toward one narrow thing.

When we train these models, we're often closer to the first student. Competitive programming is a very clean, verifiable domain, so it's natural to train on it, and in some sense we make the training look like the evaluation. Then you see the benchmark result and it's impressive. But the same model can do something strange in a real task, like fixing a bug, introducing a second bug, and then, when you point out the second bug, bringing the first one back. That doesn't match the picture of something that's superhuman at programming across the board.

So it's real progress, and I don't want to dismiss it. I just think the generalization of these models is still much worse than people's, and the evals make that hard to see.

r001.rationale: The student analogy says someone who does quite well after a hundred hours may have broader ability than someone shaped by ten thousand hours of narrow practice.

r002.rationale: The response says models are closer to the extensively practiced student and that competitive programming is a clean, verifiable domain on which they are naturally trained.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it's real evidence, but it's narrower evidence than it first looks. Competitive programming problems ask you to take a few known ideas and combine them in a configuration you haven't seen before. If a system does that reliably, it has learned something about how to reason through a problem, not just recall an answer. That matters.

The part I'd be careful about is what we're really measuring. These problems are well-defined, they have clean correctness checks, and a lot of similar material exists in the world. So a high score could reflect deep generalization, or it could reflect dense coverage of the problem space. Those two would look the same on the scoreboard.

So the question I'd ask is less "can it solve hard puzzles?" and more "does the ability hold when the problem is vague, when the specification keeps changing, and when nobody has written the solution down before?" Real-world work looks much more like that. If the competitive programming skill carries over to those conditions, then I'd take it as a meaningful sign. If it only works inside the benchmark's shape, it's a useful tool but not yet evidence of general capability.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s impressive, but you have to ask what exactly it’s evidence for. If a model solves a very difficult programming problem, that demonstrates an ability to do something genuinely difficult. But it doesn’t automatically tell you how that ability will transfer to a different setting.

With a human, if someone is exceptionally good at competitive programming, you would expect them to be able to learn a lot of other technical things. You’re using their performance as evidence about something more general. With an AI, that inference is less straightforward, especially if you’ve trained it very extensively on precisely this kind of problem.

Competitive programming also gives you a very clear objective. Here’s the problem, here are the constraints, your program either passes the tests or it doesn’t. In other work, figuring out what problem to solve can be a large part of the difficulty.

So I would take it seriously as evidence of capability. But I’d want to see what happens when you move away from the things the model has practiced. How much help does it need? How quickly does it learn? That’s where you start to find out how general the capability really is.

r001.rationale: The response says extensive practice on these problems makes broader transfer less straightforward to infer, but it does not state that comparable performance with little practice would be stronger evidence.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the inference is less straightforward when an AI has been trained extensively on precisely this kind of problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s impressive, but the question is how much it generalizes. With humans, if somebody is exceptionally good at competitive programming, you would expect them to be quite capable at other things too. With models, that connection seems less reliable. You can have a model that solves these very difficult programming problems and then struggles with something much more mundane in an actual software project.

Imagine two students. One has spent years practicing competitive programming, solving thousands and thousands of problems. The other has practiced much less, but reaches a similar level. They get the same score, but you would probably draw different conclusions about their underlying abilities and how quickly they could learn something else.

So the training matters. If we put a huge amount of effort into training on a particular kind of problem, then success on that kind of problem is evidence of an ability, but we still need to understand its scope. Competitive programming is especially convenient because you can check whether the answer is correct. That makes it a very attractive target for training.

The thing I would want to know is: what happens when you move away from that target? How much of the improvement carries over to situations that weren’t directly rewarded? That’s where you learn something about the breadth of the capability.

Success there suggests the models can do more than recall patterns. At the same time, it is a specific, well-defined setting. The interesting question is how reliably that reasoning carries over to unfamiliar problems where the goal and the feedback are less clear.

terra-5.6.text:
I think competitive programming is a very interesting benchmark because it demands a lot of different cognitive abilities at once. You have to understand a problem precisely, decompose it, come up with an algorithm, reason about edge cases, and then implement it without making mistakes. So when models get good at it, it is meaningful evidence that they’re acquiring fairly general reasoning capabilities—not just memorizing code snippets.

But it’s still a narrow, well-specified environment. The bigger question is how reliably those capabilities transfer to messier, more open-ended problems in the real world.

luna-5.6.text: I think it’s a very significant piece of evidence, because competitive programming requires abstraction, planning, precise reasoning, and the ability to turn an idea into a working artifact. It’s not just pattern matching in the ordinary sense. But it’s also not the same as demonstrating general intelligence. The models are operating in a very well-defined environment, with clear objectives and automatic verification, and they can often use search or generate many candidate solutions. So I would regard it as evidence that their reasoning abilities are becoming genuinely powerful, while still being careful not to extrapolate too directly from that benchmark to every aspect of intelligence.
